title: Hello, my name is Ani
goal: Greet anyone safely, say your name, ask other people's names, and say your first correct Bulgarian sentence — one that uses the word "is" but never puts it first.
bekal: greet formally and informally, and know the difference
say your name in two ways
ask other people's names and jobs
use the six forms of the verb **съм** in the right position
say thank you, excuse me, and you're welcome

dialogs.title: Диалог — First day of the course
dialogs.intro: Ani, a student from Indonesia, walks into a Bulgarian class in Sofia and sits next to someone she doesn't know. Watch where the little words **съм** and **е** go — neither of them ever stands at the start of a sentence.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.literal: be-healthy-(formal)! I — am — Ivan. and — you?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: My name is Ani. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: call — myself — Ani. pleasant — to-me — is.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. Are you a student?
lines.literal: also — to — me — to-me — is — pleasant. you — student-(f) — (question) — are?

lines.speaker: Ани:
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. What about you?

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: I'm not a student. I'm a teacher.
lines.literal: I — not — am — student. teacher — am.

lines.speaker: Иван:
lines.id: You're welcome. Have a nice day, Ani!

notes: **Bulgarian has a word for "is", and you must use it.** Just like English — and unlike Russian. *Аз съм студент* — "I am a student". Leaving out *съм* isn't just casual; the sentence is incomplete. ⚠️ If you've learned some Russian, your instinct may be to write *Аз студент* — and that's wrong.

**But съм can never stand at the start of a sentence.** *Съм студент* is wrong, even though the meaning is clear. It belongs to a group of little words that always lean on something before them — Bulgarian grammar calls them *клитики* (clitics). If you want to drop *аз*, another word has to move to the front: **Студентка съм.** Both are correct and mean the same; *Аз съм студентка* just puts a bit more weight on "I".

**Здравейте is formal; Здравей and Здрасти are casual.** Use Здравейте with strangers, older people, teachers, officials — anyone you call *вие*. Здравей (*zdra-VEY*) is for one friend, and Здрасти (*ZDRAS-tee*) is even more relaxed. ⚠️ Saying Здрасти to a passport officer sounds like a child patting an adult on the shoulder.

**Казвам се literally means "I call myself".** Not "my name is". The *се* means "oneself", and you'll see it stuck to verbs all the time. To ask back, just say **А вие?** — no need to repeat the whole sentence.

**Ли is a question mark in the form of a word.** Bulgarian doesn't flip the word order to ask a question the way English does ("you are" → "are you"). Instead it puts *ли* right after **the word being asked about**. *Вие студентка ли сте?* asks whether she is a student; *Вие ли сте студентка?* asks whether **she** is the student. Moving it moves the target of the question.

**Извинете and Съжалявам both mean "sorry", but they're not equally heavy.** Извинете (*eez-vee-NEH-teh*) is for small things: interrupting, squeezing past, guessing wrong. Съжалявам (*să-zha-LYA-vam*) literally means "I regret" and is for real mistakes or for offering condolences.

**Моля: one word, three jobs.** It means "please", "here you are", and "you're welcome" all at once. Said on its own with a rising tone — *Моля?* — it means "Sorry? Could you repeat that?" You'll use it dozens of times a day.
**Няма нищо literally means "there isn't nothing" — a double negative.** Bulgarian stacks negatives, and that's the correct form; Unit 13 covers it in full. For now, learn it as one fixed chunk.

grammars.title: Съм — the verb "to be"
body: This is the most important verb in Bulgarian and it's irregular, so learn it right now. Its forms look nothing like each other — just like *am / is / are* in English.
after: To make it negative, just put **не** right in front: *не съм, не си, не е, не сме, не сте, не са*. And unlike the positive form, **не съм can** start a sentence, because now *не* is the first word: *Не съм студент.*

grammars.title: The word-order rule that decides everything
body: Bulgarian has a set of small unstressed words — *съм, се, ми, те, го, ли* and friends. They all obey one single rule: **they can never be the first word in a sentence.** Everything else you can arrange fairly freely.
after: The easiest way to remember it: **a Bulgarian sentence never opens with an unstressed word.** If one of the little words is about to end up in front, push any stressed word ahead of it as a buffer.

blocks.text: These ten phrases cover almost all the small talk of your first day. Learn them as whole chunks; the grammar will untangle itself in the coming units.
Note **Добър ден**: it isn't limited to a narrow "afternoon" slot. From morning to early evening, whenever you're unsure which greeting to use, say *Добър ден* and you'll never be wrong.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Shaking your head means YES
items: This isn't a joke or a tourist legend. In Bulgaria **the head movement for "yes" is a side-to-side shake**, and "no" is a single upward nod, often with a little *ts* sound. The exact opposite of what you're used to.

On day one the effect is very real: you ask "Is there a room free?", the clerk shakes his head, you turn to leave — when he's just said yes. While you're new, **always rely on the words *да* and *не*, not the head**, and give your own answers in words, not gestures.

Bulgarians who deal with foreigners a lot sometimes flip their gestures on purpose to help you — which only makes things more confusing. When in doubt, just ask: *Да или не?* (da EE-lee neh) — "Yes or no?"

sections.title: You can already read more than you think

blocks.text: Before moving on, test yourself on the ten words below. They're all borrowed from European languages and you already know them in English — the only obstacle is the alphabet. Cover the right-hand column.
Ten words in two minutes, without memorizing anything. That's how Cyrillic works: once the letters stick, hundreds of words open up at once.

vocab.en: please; here you are; you're welcome

exercises.prompt: Translate into Bulgarian. Remember: the word "is/am/are" must be there, but never first.
Fill in the right form of съм.
Put the words in the right order. Remember the rule for the little words.
Choose the right phrase. Write the answer in Cyrillic.
items: You walk into the lecturers' office at nine in the morning. You say ____.
You didn't catch what someone said. You say ____.
You step on someone's foot on the tram. You say ____.
Someone has just helped you. You say ____.
You leave the office, formally. You say ____.

answers: Здравейте! — Казвам се Ани. — Студентка съм. — Той не е учител. — Вие студент ли сте? — Довиждане!
Казвам се Ани. — Аз не съм студент. — Приятно ми е. — Вие студентка ли сте? — Всичко е наред.
Добро утро — Моля? — Извинете — Благодаря — Довиждане
